title: Premonition
full_review:
If movie exhibitors still programmed double features, Sandra Bullock's latest vehicle would make a dandy companion to her last big film, "The Lake House." In each, her character was caught in a perplexing time warp, though "The Lake House" was primarily a romance.

"Premonition" (MGM/Hyde Park/TriStar) is an effective, fairly tense, thriller about a dutiful wife (Bullock) who learns that her husband, Jim (Julian McMahon from TV's "Nip/Tuck"), has died in a car accident while on a business trip. (Bullock's silent processing of the sorrowful news when a police officer comes to her door is beautifully conveyed.)

The stunned Linda goes through the myriad stages of grief as she breaks the news to her daughters, calls on her mother and friends for emotional support, and tries to grapple with the unbelievable.

But lo and behold, she wakes up in the morning to the surprise of her life. Jim's suitcase and other items are in their usual places, and there he is, drinking his coffee at the kitchen counter as if nothing has happened. The events of the day before were apparently just a dream, Linda's quizzical gaze suggests. But were they? Not to give too much away, because each revelation -- improbable though most of them are -- is carefully revealed, but Linda does figure out fairly early on that the dreadful event will happen a few days hence.

This is the kind of film where red herrings abound, and just about everyone around poor Linda looks conspiratorial. And that includes Jim, who (for reasons that eventually become clear) seems enigmatically detached; her mother (Kate Nelligan) and her best friend (Nia Long); and even her two little girls, one of whom cuts herself running through a glass door, emerging like a little she-devil!

Serious suspension of disbelief is required on the viewer's part. Why does Linda coolly seek out an extremely creepy doctor (Peter Stormare) when she has already experienced him (in the future) fiendishly strapping her down and administering an injection? Why does she look so panicked when a page in a phone book is ripped out when all she has to do is dial "411" instead?

But plot holes aside, it must be said that director Mennan Yapo directs with great skill, Bullock is riveting as she gradually pieces together the mystifying events around her, and there's even that rare occurrence: a fairly positive priest character to whom Linda turns when all else fails.

Oddly, it's the priest who's a treasure trove of historical trivia about past instances of crystal ball-gazing, and when he gets down to the more priestly advice, it's the most hackneyed of platitudes, but nonetheless, he's a nice cinematic anomaly.

The flagged elements below which necessitate the adult classification notwithstanding, the film is probably unobjectionable for mature teens, as sexual elements are nil and violence is minimal.

The film contains a few instances of profanity and expletives, a horrific car collision and a couple of minor accidents involving blood, mild innuendo, and suggestion of adultery.

The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
